description:
What happens when governments stop using the law to protect their citizens, and starts using it to punish them instead? This practice, known as Lawfare, can be hard to spot. Understanding that laws are not inherently neutral, but rather made to benefit their makers, is the first step to recognizing and fighting against lawfare in your own country.  

Cyanne E. Loyle is the Board of Visitors Professor of Political Science and International Affairs at the Pennsylvania State University and a Research Professor at the Peace Research Institute Oslo. Her research is motivated by a desire to better understand and contribute to the prevention of violent conflict. To advance this end, Dr. Loyle studies the use and misuse of judicial institutions by governments and armed non-state actors to hold human rights violators to account, punish political enemies, and consolidate power. title: How governments turn against us—without breaking the law | Cyanne Loyle | TEDxPSU

author: TEDx Talks
description: The Cost of the Game explores what it means to play a sport competitively, beyond winning matches or medals. From my experience as a student and volleyball player, I share the often unseen sacrifices: waking up very early, spending long hours at school, training late into the night, and dedicating weekends to tournaments instead of resting. While only the achievements are visible from the outside, behind the scenes there is exhaustion, emotional pressure, and moments of loneliness. I also discuss a significant personal cost: how sports became an escape when I felt distant from my family, taking up time that could have been spent with them. This talk isn't meant to suggest that sports are bad, but rather to highlight the importance of balance. It's about learning to pursue dreams without losing the relationships that matter most, and understanding that growing up also means knowing when to stop and reconnect with those around us. In this thought-provoking TEDxAMU talk, Hammad Rahman uses the concept of variables from the world of technology and problem-solving to explain how small decisions, habits, and perspectives can shape the trajectory of our lives.

Drawing parallels between coding and human behavior, Hammad explains that success, growth, and impact often depend on the “variables” we choose to prioritize — the people we surround ourselves with, the questions we ask, the mindset we develop, and the risks we are willing to take. When these variables are intentional and aligned with our goals, the outcomes can be transformative.

This talk encourages us to rethink the way we approach challenges. Instead of focusing only on outcomes, Hammad invites us to focus on the inputs — the daily choices, the environment, and the mindset that quietly influence the results we see over time.

In this insightful talk, Priyanka Ganguly reflects on a journey shaped by three powerful principles: gratitude, compassion, and resilience. Growing up in a small town where opportunities were limited for girls, she was encouraged by her family to pursue education and independence. These early values became the foundation that guided her through multiple career transitions across industries—from aviation to education and corporate leadership.

Along the way, she encountered challenges, biases, and unexpected changes. Instead of resisting them, she learned to adapt, stay curious, and continuously learn and unlearn. Her story highlights how resilience and strong values can help individuals navigate change, build meaningful careers, and grow beyond societal expectations.

What happens when you choose courage over comfort?

In this inspiring talk, Jasmeet Arneja shares her journey from being a school student to representing India on international fashion stages. What began as a random opportunity in a school fashion show soon turned into a life-changing decision that pushed her beyond her comfort zone.

At just 16, she took a leap of faith into the world of pageantry with no connections, no roadmap, and no guarantees. That decision led her to represent India in global competitions across Europe and appear in international media. But behind the glamour were years of discipline, rejection, pressure, and self-doubt.

Through her story, Jasmeet highlights a deeper message: success alone does not define fulfillment. True growth comes from self-awareness, resilience, and the courage to be authentic in a world that constantly demands conformity.

title: Courage to Step Out and Shine Your Light | Jasmeet Arneja | TEDxModern School Faridabad Youth

From humble beginnings and personal struggles to moments of uncertainty and rebuilding, he reflects on how consistency and perseverance can shape one’s destiny more than intelligence or circumstance.

Through real-life experiences, he highlights the importance of developing inner strength, maintaining honesty in relationships, and finding purpose in helping others. The talk also explores how setbacks, failures, and even moments of vulnerability can become the foundation for growth and leadership.

He introduces the concept of the “Visibility Paradox” and the “Power Paradox,” explaining how technology and influence are growing exponentially, while human values, responsibility, and inner depth struggle to keep pace.

Drawing on examples from history and entrepreneurship, Swwapnil highlights how true transformation begins not with external achievements but with character, values, and self-awareness. He emphasizes that intelligence alone is not enough—wisdom, responsibility, and integrity are what truly shape the future.

As AI, innovation, and digital systems reshape the world, the real question becomes:
Are humans growing internally as fast as the power they are creating externally?

author: TEDx Talks
description:
In this talk, Shubhanshi reframes sustainability as a crisis of broken relationships rather than broken systems. Drawing from the Bhagavad Gita, she introduces the idea of Akash; the invisible field of connection often missing from modern climate discourse.

Through personal stories, from disappearing Ayurvedic plants in her village to the coal fires of Jharia, she shows how ecological collapse mirrors inner fragmentation. Weaving indigenous wisdom, the story of Annapoorna, and her work documenting Chhau dancers in her film Natok, she argues that sustainability is not just environmental protection, but relational restoration.

The crisis is not only about carbon.
It is about restoring dialogue; between systems, communities, and ourselves. Sustainability is not about saving the Earth. It is about rebuilding our relationship with it.
